country.comment: The study examines domestic piped water distribution, consumption, rationing, and neighbourhood inequalities in Nairobi County, Kenya.
country.where_found: PDF p. 2, Title and Abstract; PDF p. 3, Section 2.1

effect_estimate.comment: Across 2,380 residential itineraries (2008–2018), the multivariable negative binomial linear mixed-effects model (Table 4) estimated higher monthly per capita piped water consumption relative to low-income areas (R4, n = 252; average 827 L/capita/month, 60% <1,500 L/capita/month) in high-income (R1, n = 534; RR = 5.78, 95% CI: 5.34–6.25, p < 0.001; 13,087 L/capita/month, 7% <1,500 L), middle-income (R2, n = 772; RR = 3.80, 95% CI: 3.52–4.10, p < 0.001; 6,240 L/capita/month, 12% <1,500 L), and middle/low-income areas (R3, n = 822; RR = 1.65, 95% CI: 1.53–1.79, p < 0.001; 1,697 L/capita/month, 36% <1,500 L). Older settlements had lower consumption than post-2014 settlements (1975–1990 RR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.60–0.65, p < 0.001; 1990–2000 RR = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.85–0.89, p < 0.001; 2000–2014 RR = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.94–0.99, p < 0.001; pre-1975 RR = 0.54, 95% CI: 0.53–0.56, p = 0.425), as did more populous itineraries (RR = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.71–0.93, p < 0.001). Under 2016–2018 utility rationing schedules, R4 received more supply hours/week (78 h) than R3 (65 h), R1 (59 h), and R2 (50 h) yet remained water-insufficient; KSCBS validation (n = 1,137 households) showed secure tenure ranged from 85% in R1 to 48% in R4. Non-revenue water averaged 3.5 billion L/month (29% of supply), exceeding the 1.5 billion L/month needed for universal >=1,500 L/capita/month consumption.
effect_estimate.value: Compared to low-income residential zones (R4, reference; mean 827 L/capita/month; 60% <1,500 L/capita/month), monthly per capita piped water consumption across 2,380 residential itineraries (2008–2018) was higher in high-income zones (R1: Rate Ratio [RR] = 5.78, 95% CI: 5.34–6.25, p < 0.001; mean 13,087 L/capita/month; 7% <1,500 L), middle-income zones (R2: RR = 3.80, 95% CI: 3.52–4.10, p < 0.001; mean 6,240 L/capita/month; 12% <1,500 L), and middle/low-income zones (R3: RR = 1.65, 95% CI: 1.53–1.79, p < 0.001; mean 1,697 L/capita/month; 36% <1,500 L). Settlements built 1975–1990 (RR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.60–0.65, p < 0.001), 1990–2000 (RR = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.85–0.89, p < 0.001), and 2000–2014 (RR = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.94–0.99, p < 0.001) had lower consumption than post-2014 settlements, and higher itinerary population reduced per capita consumption (RR = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.71–0.93, p < 0.001). Low-income zones received the longest scheduled weekly supply under 2016–2018 utility rationing (78 h/week vs. 59 h in R1 and 50 h in R2) and had the lowest household tenure security (48% vs. 85% in R1; n = 1,137 households).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Observational ecological/cross-sectional analytical study (design ceiling <= 2). Rated 1 (documented statistical/descriptive association) because the authors test aggregate statistical associations between municipal/utility residential land-use categories (explicitly treated as a socio-economic proxy), built-settlement age, rationing hours, and per capita consumption, and descriptively cross-tabulate KSCBS tenure security across residential classes, while assuming connection modes within itineraries and inferring underlying legal/institutional drivers (e.g., unenforced kiosk tariffs, state reluctance to legitimise informal tenure).

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines municipal master-planning and residential land-use classifications (1973 Metropolitan Growth Strategy, 1979 land-use maps, 1985 water distribution plan, and 2014 Integrated Urban Development Master Plan / 2018 land-use zones R1–R4, including unauthorised shanty dwellings) guiding piped network allocation and connection modes (planning, zoning), utility billing/rationing geographical itineraries and grid boundaries (service_area), household security of tenure across R1–R4 in KSCBS (tenure), and NCWSC's domestic block tariff schedule and unenforced kiosk retail rates (fees).

sample_size.comment: Out of 3,000 NCWSC billing itineraries, 554 lacked geographical coordinates and were excluded, leaving 2,538 itineraries (2,380 residential itineraries—averaging ~700 residents each—and 158 non-residential itineraries) analysed with monthly consumption records from 2008 to 2018 (plus Nov 2016–May 2018 reservoir production/NRW data and Oct 2016–Dec 2018 rationing schedules). In addition, 1,137 household respondents across 7 Nairobi sublocations from the 2012–2013 KSCBS were analysed to validate residential categories (R1 n = 60, R2 n = 170, R3 n = 161, R4 n = 746).

study_design.comment: Ecological spatio-temporal observational study integrating monthly utility billing/consumption records (2008–2018), reservoir production/non-revenue water records (2016–2018), rationing schedules (2016–2018), 1985 vs. 2018 land-use/network maps, WorldPop gridded population, and GHS built-settlement age across 2,380 residential itineraries analysed via GIS spatial queries and a multivariable negative binomial linear mixed-effects model (with year as a random effect), supplemented by cross-tabulation with cross-sectional household survey data (2012–2013 KSCBS).
